paragraphs.heading: The supreme law
paragraphs.text: The Constitution of the United States is the highest law of the country. It began with seven articles that laid out the basic structure of the federal government. It replaced the nation's first constitution, the Articles of Confederation, on March 4, 1789. Today it is the oldest written and codified national constitution still in force anywhere in the world.

paragraphs.heading: The first attempt
paragraphs.text: The Articles of Confederation were drafted by a committee of the Second Continental Congress in 1777 and adopted by Congress that November. Getting all 13 states to ratify them took more than three years, until March 1, 1781. The Articles gave the central government very little power. Congress could make some decisions but had no way to enforce them, and most choices, even changes to the Articles, needed the approval of every state legislature.

paragraphs.heading: No money, no defense
paragraphs.text: George Washington summed up the main problem as "no money". Congress could print money, but it was worthless, and it could borrow but not repay. No state paid its share of taxes and some paid nothing, and by 1786 the country faced default on its debts. The army had just 625 men, its soldiers went unpaid, and when Barbary pirates seized American merchant ships, the Treasury had nothing to pay ransom with.

paragraphs.heading: States going their own way
paragraphs.text: The Articles were also failing to unite states with very different interests. Some states broke the 1783 Treaty of Paris with Britain, and New York and South Carolina kept prosecuting Loyalists and taking their land. State legislatures set their own embargoes, dealt directly with foreign powers, raised armies and even made war. During Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts, Congress could give the threatened state no money, so General Benjamin Lincoln had to raise funds from Boston merchants for a volunteer army.

paragraphs.heading: Framing a new plan
paragraphs.text: Many of the Founding Fathers drafted a new constitution at the Constitutional Convention, which met at Independence Hall in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787. This drafting is often called the framing. The framers drew on English common law and on Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke and Montesquieu.

paragraphs.heading: How the articles divide power
paragraphs.text: The first three articles follow the idea of separation of powers, which splits government into three branches. The legislature is Congress, which has two chambers; the president leads the executive; and the Supreme Court sits at the top of the judiciary. Articles IV, V and VI deal with federalism: they describe the rights and duties of state governments and how the states relate to the federal government, and they set out how the Constitution can be amended. Article VII describes how the Constitution was to be ratified.

paragraphs.heading: Amendments
paragraphs.text: Since 1789 the Constitution has been amended 27 times. Unlike changes to many constitutions elsewhere, these amendments are attached to the end of the document. The first ten, together called the Bill of Rights, protect individual liberty and justice and limit what government can do. Amendments 13 to 15 are called the Reconstruction Amendments, and most later ones widen civil rights protections.
